newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: UN court to sentence Serb for war crimes on Monday.
newsitem.headline: UN court to sentence Serb for war crimes on Monday.

text.p: The U.N. war crimes tribunal for former Yugoslavia will pronounce its first sentence after a full trial on Monday when it decides punishment for a Bosnian Serb convicted of killing and torturing Moslems.
Dusan Tadic, 41, was found guilty on May 7 of taking part in a Serb "ethnic cleansing" campaign against Bosnian Moslems in Prijedor, northwestern Bosnia in the early stages of the war in 1992.

The Prijedor purge was one of the worst atrocities of the war. Non-Serbs, mostly Moslems but also Croats, were herded into three notorious prison camps to be beaten, kept in inhumane conditions and, in some cases, executed.
Tadic, who has already spent three years in custody, faces a maximum sentence of life imprisonment, a term demanded by the tribunal's prosecutors. The court cannot impose a death penalty.
Tadic has consistently denied all charges, claiming he was a hapless victim of the Moslems' desire to find a scapegoat for their suffering at the hands of the Serbs.
His lawyers have appealed against the guilty verdict.
Sentencing on Tadic coincides with a new toughening of efforts by NATO-led peacekeeping troops in Bosnia to apprehend fugitive indicted war criminals.
Last week, crack British troops in Prijedor shot dead regional police chief Simo Drljaca after he resisted capture and arrested hospital director Milan Kovacevic.
Both were the subject of secret tribunal indictments in connection with the 1992 events in Prijedor. Kovacevic is now jailed in The Hague awaiting trial.

"This was a signal. This was a start. These people have got to face justice, and we are determined internationally that they are going to do so," British Defence Secretary George Robertson said on Sunday.

The NATO swoop has stirred speculation that the two most wanted war-crimes indictees -- former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic and military chief General Ratko Mladic -- may also be snatched soon.

But the killing of Drljaca and arrest of Kovacevic has also aggravated tension between the NATO alliance and Russia, which denounced the operation as a "cowboy raid". Russia has troops in the peacekeeping force.
The U.N. tribunals for Yugoslavia and Rwanda mark the first attempt to try war criminals before an international panel of judges since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials after World War Two.
The International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia has publicly indicted 76 people so far, most of them Serbs, but has only 10 in custody in The Hague.
